# Mild traumatic brain injury

## Definition and Epidemiology

Traumatic brain injuries (TBIs) refer to any injury in which an external force applied to the head results in structural injury or physiological brain disruption1. These injuries are typically categorized by severity as being mild, moderate, or severe. The precise definitions for TBI and its subcategories of severity vary across sources based on the injury’s specific causes and symptoms2.

The ambiguity of defining TBI is particularly prominent for mild traumatic brain injuries (mTBIs)3. One common definition that is used to categorize a TBI as mild by sources such as the World Health Organization (WHO)’s Collaborating Centre for Neurotrauma Task Force4 and the United States Department of Veterans Affairs5 is that the injury must reveal no abnormalities on traditional methods of structural brain imaging, no more than 30 minutes of lost consciousness following the impact, no more than 24 hours of altered mental state or confusion, and a score above 13 on the 15-point Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS)1. The GCS is a clinical tool that examines a patient’s eye-opening, verbal, and motor responses to commands and physical stimulation to determine their precise level of consciousness along the spectrum of completely non-responsive to completely responsive6.

The term mTBI is also commonly used interchangeably with the term concussion1,7, however, some organizations believe the term concussion should only be used to describe a specific form of (typically sports-related) mTBI, or to describe a distinct injury that shares some overlap in causes and outcomes as mTBI8. Others also believe the ambiguity associated with the term concussion is sufficient reason to not use it at all9.


A recent article published in JAMA insights outlined the state of clinical post-mTBI care and management as of 201921. Potentially as a result of the complexity of the condition, there are currently no therapeutic interventions that are known to mitigate the consequences of mTBI; the resolution of symptoms is the primary metric used to determine the pace at which an mTBI patient may resume tasks of varying cognitive and physical demand19,21. Stricter caution is used in cases where there is higher risk of sustaining a subsequent concussion or injury, such as for athletes, military personnel, and the elderly.

The high prevalence of mTBIs, their potentially serious and persistent outcomes, and their lack of effective treatments and therapies position them as a leading global health concern and an important priority for research.


## Outcomes

Though mTBIs are the least harmful form of TBI, they are thought to make up between 80-90% of all TBIs1 and afflict approximately 600 per 100,000 people every year7. A study by Boak et al. reported that upwards of 15% of children in Ontario sustain an mTBI each year [@LUZM3UW8#Boak_Etal_2020]. While the majority of mTBIs result in transient, self-limiting symptoms which resolve within 7-10 days8, approximately 10-20% of all mTBIs can lead to long-lasting neurological, cognitive, and behavioural symptoms including depression10, anxiety11, headaches12, dizziness13, fatigue, increased irritability11, difficulties in concentration14, impairments in memory, abnormal sleeping patterns15, emotional volatility16, stress intolerance17, decreased reaction times18, and visual tracking ability18, which may take months or years to resolve, or may never resolve at all1,14,19. Patients with mTBI have also been identified as having higher incidence rates of conditions such as dementia7 and chronic traumatic encephalopathy20. In approximately 25% of cases [@5YF45S66#Fried_Etal_2022], symptoms following mTBI persist for several months or years after the initial trauma. 


## Mechanisms of damage

Pathological sequelae of TBI are commonly split into primary and secondary damage phases22. The primary damage phase refers to the immediate effects of the mechanical disruption of the brain, while the secondary damage phase encompasses longer lasting cellular and molecular mechanisms that are initiated by the consequences of the primary damage23. The mechanisms relating the initial trauma to the consequences of mTBI are briefly summarized in Figure 1 and described in more detail in the following subsections.


### Primary biomechanical mechanisms of damage

Though the mechanisms by which trauma to the head can result in injury to the brain are not completely known, novel advances in our understanding of the contributing biomechanical, cellular, and molecular processes are continuously being made.

Compared to TBIs of higher severities, the major effects of the primary damage phase of mTBIs are less defined by direct trauma to the brain and more defined by the straining and shearing forces generated by the rapid changes in the brain’s rotational and linear acceleration24. These extreme changes in acceleration generate intracranial pressure gradients that permeate through the brain1 and cause irreversible damage to critical brain structures1.


### Secondary cellular and molecular mechanisms of damage

The initial mechanical forces of an mTBI can trigger secondary cellular and molecular processes that perpetuate brain degeneration or hinder brain recovery for years after the trauma. This secondary damage is composed of several complex mechanisms whose interactions are the subject of current investigations, and include oxidative stress22, mitochondrial disruption26, inflammation27, axon degeneration28, and cellular apoptosis25,29. 

TBIs can cause damage through the transient disruption of cell membranes, which can create imbalances in intra- and extra-cellular concentrations of ions and neurotransmitters30. Acutely after an injury, neuronal presynaptic terminals can aberrantly release glutamate, resulting in disrupted neuronal communication across the brain. The excessive extracellular concentrations of glutamate are exacerbated by the widespread dysfunction of glutamate transporters in the acute phase of the injury31. Potassium can also be released by neurons in a manner proportionate to the severity of the trauma32, which can further exacerbate the disruptions in inter-neuronal signaling. 

TBIs can also result in abnormal buildups of intracellular calcium ions, which can in turn trigger excessive mitochondrial calcium uptake and subsequent impaired mitochondrial function30. 

Another consequence of TBI is the so-called ‘post-TBI energy crisis’30, which describes the significant drop in brain glucose uptake following injury. The mechanisms by which glucose uptake is inhibited following TBI is not known but could be attributed to any combination of impaired glucose transporter function at the blood brain barrier, impaired levels of cerebral blood flow, and cellular impairments in metabolic processing.

Overproduction of free radicals and oxidative stress as a result of intracellular calcium accumulation22 is another component by which TBIs are known to damage the brain30. While reactive oxygen species (ROS) are a normal product of the brain’s metabolic functions, TBI can result in ROS levels that are too high for homeostatic ROS scavenging molecules to mitigate33. The overabundance of ROS can go on to exacerbate brain damage by altering cell membrane permeability34, disrupting DNA repair35, and causing mitochondrial dysfunction36 among other harmful consequences.

The activation of glial cells is also recognized to be a major mechanism by which inflammation, degeneration, and repair are regulated following mTBI. At rest, astrocytes play important roles in establishing homeostatic conditions in the central nervous system, supporting neuronal function, and maintaining the integrity of the blood-brain barrier37. After a mild traumatic brain injury, astrocytes adjust their morphology and gene expression signature (a reaction known as astrogliosis38), proliferate and migrate towards damaged structures39, buffer ionic imbalances through cellular pumps and channels, and secrete both damaging and reparative cytokines and chemokines40. In more severe injury contexts, astrocytes are also capable of forming scars that protect healthy tissue from the inflammatory molecules at the sites of damaged structures41.

Microglia, the resident immune cells of the central nervous system, also have a complex role in the pathophysiology of mTBI. Under homeostatic conditions, microglia constantly survey their surrounding area for signs of trauma or pathogenic invasion using highly motile processes, which, upon detection, can induce a heterogeneous set of contextually specific and morphologically, transcriptionally, and functionally activated microglial states 42. Similar to astrocytes, microglia have both damaging and reparative functions when activated following mTBI. Reparative functions of microglia include phagocytosing cellular debris and producing scavenger receptors, anti-inflammatory cytokines, and growth factors, while damaging functions include producing pro-inflammatory cytokines and excessively phagocytosing tissues that are healthy or capable of being repaired40,43,44.

The complete interplay and ordering of the previously outlined mechanisms are complex and likely dependent on the specific combination of patient and injury factors. However, in addition to the primary mechanical forces described in the previous subsection, many of these secondary cellular and molecular processes play a significant role in mediating a major correlate of post-mTBI impairment: damage or disruption to the brain’s white matter. 


## The heterogeneity of mTBI

MTBIs can result in a wide range of symptoms, including problems with sleep, memory, behaviour, and cognition [@KJSSHI24#Corwin_Etal_2017; @ISVG4ADD#Rosenbaum_Etal_2020]. Despite the prevalence of the condition, there are currently no proven, effective treatments for persistent attention problems and cognitive symptoms following paediatric mTBI. This absence may in part be due to the treatment of mTBI as a single condition in clinical trials, despite previous studies having found the injury to be highly diverse across characteristics related to the patients, their trauma, and their symptoms [@64T9WPSQ#Yuh_Etal_2021; @R7JRSM93#Schindler_Etal_2021; @4Z2E5895#Bui_Etal_2021; @DCC2L9PL#Yeates_Etal_2019; @A9F84VB3#Visscher_Etal_2019; @YU7I35JW#Si_Etal_2018; @QPXU5WEI#Si_Etal_2018; @MLDHGQBW#Snell_Etal_2015; @HK2S6C4R#Kenzie_Etal_2017]. A more detailed summary of the existing literature on subtyping mTBI can be found in the next chapter of the book (@sec-mtbi-subtyping-literature)


Some of those previous studies attempted to understand this heterogeneity by employed clustering methodologies to identify subtypes of mTBI patients. However, limitations in the available datasets and statistical methods precluded the usage of more than only small subsets of key variables in the analyses. Traditional approaches to integrating information across diverse data-types typically result in a substantial loss of signal-to-noise ratio for each type used, which is especially problematic in the context of already-noisy biological data. More recent advances in data-integration techniques avoided this particular issue [@W9Z4CA2R#Wang_Etal_2014] but would not scale well for high-dimensional data. Within the last few years, a data-integration technique called similarity network fusion (SNF) was developed specifically for the identification of patient subtypes across high-dimensional and diverse datasets.


### Sex differences

One notable component of the heterogeneity of mTBI is the differential outcomes experienced by males and females. A search of the PubMed database for review papers in the last 10 years that have examined how sex influences clinical mTBI outcomes (search: “sex” and (“mTBI” or “mild traumatic brain injury”)) identified 8 reviews which found that females generally had worse outcomes following mTBI19,74–80, 1 review which found that males generally had worse outcomes81, two reviews reporting mixed outcomes82,83, and two reviews reporting no conclusive differences between the sexes10,84. 

Though clinical studies tend to suggest that females experience poorer outcomes than males, a recent systematic review by Gupte et al.73 examining sex differences following TBI of all severities found that in general, the opposite was true for animal studies. This review also found that the proportion of studies which reported a particular type of sex difference seemed to vary considerably with impact severity; among the 12 mTBI studies examined, 25% (n = 4) reported that females had worse outcomes and 17% (n = 2) reported that males had worse outcomes, but among the 31 moderate-severe TBI studies examined, only 10% (n = 3) reported that females had worse outcomes and 55% (n = 17) reported that males had worse outcomes. Whether this pattern was the result of chance due to the small number of mTBI studies or a reflection of a biological interaction effect of impact severity with sex remains to be determined. 

Though there are several studies which suggest that sex can influence outcomes of mTBI, it is not yet clear how or when these differences in outcomes occur. Including sex as a parameter in replicable experimental mTBI studies and examining how it interacts with other study factors will be a necessary component of future work to fully understand the pathophysiology and possible treatments of mTBI.  
## White matter vulnerability to mTBI

White matter regions of the brain, which are structures composed mainly of myelinated axons that primarily function to relay information between different brain regions, are known to be highly susceptible to both primary mechanical and secondary molecular damage processes following mTBI45–47.

Although all cells and structures in the brain are affected to some degree by the mechanical forces associated with mTBI, white matter structures are particularly vulnerable to primary damage due to their high composition of long neuronal axons45. Rather than the overt degeneration of white matter that may be more commonly seen in severe forms of TBI, mTBI often results in axon damage and axon-myelin pathology46. Diffuse axonal injury (DAI), the most common form of axonal injury associated with mild injuries, is initiated by the mechanical forces of the injury and characterized by widespread patterns of damaged axons interspersed among intact ones, typically in midline white matter tracts such as the corpus callosum and internal capsules 28,46. In cases of mTBI, axonal damage has been observed to occur without surrounding vascular damage, suggesting that axons are substantially more susceptible to these injuries than blood vessels46.

Both the mechanical action of the impact as well as the byproducts of structures that were damaged by that action can go on to initiate secondary cellular and molecular processes of brain damage25. 

Though the precise mechanisms by which secondary molecular and cellular damage and repair processes affect white matter following mTBI are not fully understood, some contributing processes have been identified. For mild brain injuries, those mechanical forces may cause axonal cytoskeleton disruption or imbalances of intra-axonal ion concentrations that primarily lead to swelling and sometimes secondary axonal disconnection. Another secondary mechanism by which white matter damage can occur is by degeneration or loss of oligodendrocyte lineage cells, which can subsequently lead to the disruption or loss of myelin46. This disruption may be initiated by a variety of mechanisms after head trauma, including glutamate excitotoxicity48, oxidative stress49, and inflammatory consequences of activated astrocytes40,50 and microglia40,51,52. 

The general progression of white matter damage following mTBI is thought to typically begin with DAI from the primary impact causing unmyelinated axon fibers to degenerate and myelinated axon fibers to become damaged at the nodes of Ranvier46. Swelling and atrophy of distal axon segments following initial damage then further disrupts surrounding myelin. Secondary processes can then initiate demyelination of intact axons and additional axonal damage, again beginning from the nodes of Ranvier46,47. Axons that are sufficiently damaged enough may become irreversibly disconnected. 

Myelin sheaths, the insulating layer of axons, are part of oligodendrocytes. Myelin plays a major role in axon vulnerability to damage: unmyelinated axons are especially susceptible to traumatic axonal injury. As well, the axon initial segment, an unmyelinated region of the beginning of an axon, is often the initial site of axon cleavage (axotomy) following traumatic axonal injury. Myelin debris is also enough to trigger the activation of microglia and infiltrating macrophages53, which may play a significant role in propagating secondary damage following mTBI. Myelin debris has also been shown to inhibit the differentiation of oligodendrocyte precursor cells, which is a necessary process for myelin regeneration54,55. 

Importantly, damage to white matter structures following mTBI has been strongly associated with the cognitive, neurological, and behavioural impairments that can follow the injury46,51,56, making them an important candidate target for the development of mTBI therapies and biomarkers. 


## Detection of post-mTBI white matter damage

The subtle white matter damage that follows mTBI is most commonly detected (in both clinical and preclinical contexts) through neuroimaging and histological analysis46. In the context of living subjects (which is the relevant context for this project), the histological approach to detecting white matter damage is not really applicable. The usage of neuroimaging (particularly MRI) for mTBI diagonosis and prognosis is described in detail in a later chapter in this book (@sec-neuroimaging).

To better detect white matter damage in patients of mTBI, advanced MRI techniques, such as diffusion tensor imaging (DTI), are being increasingly used46. Because white matter has a more fibrous structure than gray matter, the diffusion of water within it is more directional. DTI scans measure the degree of directionality, or fractional anisotropy (FA), of water molecules over the entire brain in 3D units known as voxels. In a study that collected DTI scans of 76 adults that had received an mTBI 1 to 2 weeks prior, the reduction of FA was found to be a predictive measure of long-term outcome57. Other studies have reported both increases58 and decreases59, 60 in post-TBI FA, suggesting that even the type of structural white matter changes that follow a TBI are complex and likely depend on multiple factors. Within white matter tracts that are complex and/or long-range, the accuracy of DTI in detecting abnormalities is still limited46.
